Get started with lexio

Source: vignettes/lexio.Rmd
lexio.Rmd

lexio runs an input-output model solved by preemptive (lexicographic) goal programming. You declare an input-output database that you already have and, for each satellite account (energy, jobs, emissions, …), a direction, a goal and a priority. The package chooses the sectoral output that best meets the goals, in priority order, for every ordering of the priorities, and writes every result.

This vignette runs a complete example on a three-sector database. The other vignettes cover the full specification (vignette("model-specification")), the goal programming example of Miller and Blair (vignette("miller-blair")) and the replication of the thesis that introduced the model (vignette("thesis-replication")).

The model

With n sectors and k satellite accounts, the goals form the system

Gx+d−−d+=g,G=[DI−A],x,d+,d−≥0. G x + d^- - d^+ = g, \qquad G = \begin{bmatrix} D \\ I - A \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x,\ d^+,\ d^- \ge 0 .

  • x is the gross output of each sector, the decision variable.
  • The first k rows are the satellite accounts. D holds the coefficients of each account per unit of output, so D_j x is the level of account j and b_j = D_j x_0 is its base.
  • The last n rows are the economic block, ECO: (I - A) x against the final demand f.
  • d^- and d^+ are the deviations below and above each goal g.

Each account has a direction. A floor (">=") penalizes the shortfall d^-, a ceiling ("<=") penalizes the excess d^+, and a target ("=") penalizes both. ECO is a floor on the final demand by default.

The goals are met in priority order. Each priority level is a linear program, solved with GLPK, that minimizes the penalized deviations of its goals; its optimum is then locked for the following levels. Since the order matters, the package runs, by default, all k! orderings of the accounts, with ECO fixed at the last level.

Optionally, a corridor bounds the economic deviations: d_h^-, d_h^+ <= alpha_h |g_h|, where alpha_h is a proportion declared for each sector.

A first run

1. Declare the database

The database has three sectors. Z holds the intermediate flows (row = selling sector, column = buying sector), x the gross output and f the final demand. Each satellite account is given as its level in each sector: an entrant energy source E and an incumbent I (in toe) and labour LAB (in jobs). alpha is the corridor of each sector.

library(lexio)

Z <- matrix(c(10, 15, 5,
              20, 10, 8,
               5, 10, 6), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
x <- c(100, 80, 60)
f <- c(70, 42, 39)
E_entrant <- c(2, 4, 0.6)
E_incumbent <- c(10, 16, 3)
E_labour <- c(100, 40, 120)
alpha <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.15)
sectors <- data.frame(code = c("S1", "S2", "S3"), name = c("Agriculture", "Industry", "Services"))

declare_io() receives each object under the name of what it is: Z = for flows (A = or B = for technical coefficients), E = for levels of the accounts (D = for coefficients) and corridor = for the corridor. The package computes A = Z x^-1, B = I - A and D = E x^-1.

io <- declare_io(Z = Z, x = x, f = f,
                 E = list(E = E_entrant, I = E_incumbent, LAB = E_labour),
                 corridor = alpha, sectors = sectors)
io
#> <lexio_io> 3 sectors, 3 satellite account(s): E, I, LAB | declared as Z + E | corridor: two-sided corridor 
#>   base E = D x =   6.60
#>   base I = D x =  29.00
#>   base LAB = D x = 260.00

The printout shows how the database was declared, the corridor mode and the base b_j = D_j x of each account. validate_io(io) gives the full report of the consistency checks.

2. Declare the model

The entrant energy is a floor, the incumbent energy a ceiling and labour a floor that should grow by 5%. Two scenarios give a shock equal to 5% of the joint base of the two energy sources, either to the entrant or to the incumbent.

shock <- list(type = "pooled_share", share = 0.05, pool = c("E", "I"))
model <- define_model(
  accounts = list(
    E   = list(direction = ">=", target = list(type = "base"), label = "Entrant energy", unit = "toe"),
    I   = list(direction = "<=", target = list(type = "base"), label = "Incumbent energy", unit = "toe"),
    LAB = list(direction = ">=", target = list(type = "growth", rate = 0.05), label = "Labour", unit = "jobs")
  ),
  scenarios = list(E_shock = list(E = shock),
                   I_shock = list(I = shock)),
  name = "toy"
)
model
#> <lexio_model> toy | 3 satellite account(s), 2 scenario(s), 6 priority ordering(s) | lock: auto (exact; relaxed only where GLPK fails) 
#>   E        >= base
#>   I        <= base
#>   LAB      >= base x (1 + 0.05)
#>   ECO      >= final demand f | absolute deviations | fixed at the last level
#>   corridor: as declared in the data (multiplier 1) 
#>   P01: E > I > LAB > ECO
#>   P02: E > LAB > I > ECO
#>   P03: I > E > LAB > ECO
#>   P04: I > LAB > E > ECO
#>   P05: LAB > E > I > ECO
#>   P06: LAB > I > E > ECO
#>   scenario E_shock (changes: E) 
#>   scenario I_shock (changes: I)

The goal of each account is computed from its base. In the scenario E_shock, the goal of E is b_E + 0.05 (b_E + b_I), the goal of I is its base and the goal of LAB is 1.05 b_LAB. The goals of the economic block are the final demand. build_goals() returns the whole vector g:

build_goals(io, model, "E_shock")
#> [1]   8.38  29.00 273.00  70.00  42.00  39.00

With three accounts there are 3! = 6 orderings, P01 to P06, each with four levels: the three accounts in the order of the ordering, and ECO.

3. Run 

res <- run_model(io, model, verbose = FALSE)
res
#> <lexio_results> toy | 3 sectors | 3 account(s): E, I, LAB | corridor: two-sided corridor 
#>   scenario E_shock        6 ordering(s) | all optimal | 3 distinct state(s)
#>   scenario I_shock        6 ordering(s) | all optimal | 1 distinct state(s)
#>   distinct states in total: 4 
#>   write everything with write_outputs(res, "folder")

The model ran 12 times: 2 scenarios and 6 orderings. A state is a final solution x*; different orderings may lead to the same state.

Reading the results

In R

res$summary holds four tables. runs has one row per run: the GLPK status of each level (0 = optimal), the optimum Z of each level, the change in total output and the change in each account.

runs <- res$summary$runs[, c("scenario", "label", "priorities", "status", "Z1", "Z2", "Z3", "Z4",
                             "delta_x", "delta_E", "delta_I", "delta_LAB", "state")]
runs[5:12] <- round(runs[5:12], 4)
runs
#>    scenario label        priorities status     Z1     Z2      Z3      Z4 delta_x delta_E delta_I

Printing a single run shows every level and every account:

res$runs[[3]]
#> <gp_run> toy | scenario E_shock | P03 : I > E > LAB > ECO 
#>   level 1 I            GLP_OPT    Z = 0
#>   level 2 E            GLP_OPT    Z = 1.72818
#>   level 3 LAB          GLP_OPT    Z = 30.0487
#>   level 4 ECO          GLP_OPT    Z = 12.85
#>   accounts at the last level:
#>     E        >= base 6.6            goal 8.38           achieved 6.651815       d- 1.72818      d+ 0
#>     I        <= base 29             goal 29             achieved 29             d- 0            d+ 0
#>     LAB      >= base 260            goal 273            achieved 242.9513       d- 30.0487      d+ 0
#>   ECO: shortfall sum(d-) = 12.85, excess sum(d+) = 6.81259 | delta x = -8.273668 (-3.4474%)
#>   corridor: two-sided corridor | ok: TRUE

In files

write_outputs() writes every result to a folder: a report (README.md), an Excel workbook (results.xlsx), the tables as CSV files and, for each run, a folder with the results of every level.

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "toy_results")
write_outputs(res, out)
list.files(out)
#>  [1] "account_goals.csv"   "inputs"              "level_results.csv"   "levels.csv"         
#>  [5] "orderings.csv"       "README.md"           "results.rds"         "results.xlsx"       
#>  [9] "runs"                "session.txt"         "states.csv"          "x_star_all_runs.csv"
list.files(file.path(out, "runs", "E_shock", "P03_I-E-LAB"))
#> [1] "all_levels.csv" "level_1.csv"    "level_2.csv"    "level_3.csv"    "level_4.csv"   
#> [6] "x_star.csv"

all_levels.csv has one row per row of G (the accounts, then the sectors) and, side by side, the goal and the result of every level of the run:

read.csv(file.path(out, "runs", "E_shock", "P03_I-E-LAB", "all_levels.csv"))[, 1:13]
#>   row notation             name   block      g  level1_Gx level1_d_minus level1_d_plus  level1_x
#> 1   E      xD1   Entrant energy account   8.38   6.583151       1.796849          0.00        NA
#> 2   I      xD2 Incumbent energy account  29.00  29.000000       0.000000          0.00        NA
#> 3 LAB      xD3           Labour account 273.00 271.945491       1.054509          0.00        NA
#> 4  S1      f'1      Agriculture     ECO  70.00  70.000000       0.000000          0.00 100.23035
#> 5  S2      f'2         Industry     ECO  42.00  39.642493       2.357507          0.00  78.31513
#> 6  S3      f'3         Services     ECO  39.00  44.850000       0.000000          5.85  66.27879
#>    level2_Gx level2_d_minus level2_d_plus level2_x
#> 1   6.651815       1.728185      0.000000       NA
#> 2  29.000000       0.000000      0.000000       NA
#> 3 242.951285      30.048715      0.000000       NA
#> 4  63.000000       7.000000      0.000000 92.72909
#> 5  48.812589       0.000000      6.812589 85.18153
#> 6  33.150000       5.850000      0.000000 53.81572

The notation follows the system above: xD_j is the level of account j (D_j x) and f'_h is row h of (I - A) x, the net output of sector h, whose goal is its final demand.

In Excel

results.xlsx (or write_excel(res, "file.xlsx")) holds the same results in one workbook:

Sheet Content
about the model, the scenarios, the orderings, the notation and what each sheet holds
runs, levels, goals, states the four summary tables
final_<scenario> the last level of every ordering, side by side: g, then Gx, d_minus, d_plus and x of each ordering
Gx_<scenario> g, the Gx of each ordering and Gx - g
x_<scenario> the base output x0, the output x* of each ordering and delta_x
<scenario>_<ordering> one sheet per run: every row of G at every level, side by side 
readxl::excel_sheets(file.path(out, "results.xlsx"))
#>  [1] "about"         "runs"          "levels"        "goals"         "states"        "final_E_shock"
#>  [7] "Gx_E_shock"    "x_E_shock"     "final_I_shock" "Gx_I_shock"    "x_I_shock"     "E_shock_P01"  
#> [13] "E_shock_P02"   "E_shock_P03"   "E_shock_P04"   "E_shock_P05"   "E_shock_P06"   "I_shock_P01"  
#> [19] "I_shock_P02"   "I_shock_P03"   "I_shock_P04"   "I_shock_P05"   "I_shock_P06"

The same model from files

A study is usually kept in files: a folder with the database (or an .xlsx workbook) and a model.yml with the model. lexio_template() writes this example in that format, with a commented model.yml, to be copied and filled in with your own data.

study <- file.path(tempdir(), "my_study")
lexio_template(study)
list.files(study, recursive = TRUE)
#> [1] "base/corridor.csv" "base/E.csv"        "base/f.csv"        "base/sectors.csv" 
#> [5] "base/x.csv"        "base/Z.csv"        "model.yml"
res_files <- run_model(file.path(study, "model.yml"), verbose = FALSE)
identical(res_files$summary$runs$Z4, res$summary$runs$Z4)
#> [1] TRUE
